Angular_Leaf_Spot_Of_Strawberry.quote: Symptoms first appear as tiny water-soaked lesions on the undersides of leaves, and as these lesions enlarge, they become delineated by small veins and appear angular.
Calyxes can also become infected and turn brown or black and dry up, resulting in unmarketable fruit when severe.

Anthracnose.quote: As the disease progresses and fruit ripens, fruit lesions become sunken and brown, and then an orange coloration develops in the sunken area as spores are produced.
Dark elongated lesions develop on petioles and runner stems.
Crown rot may first be seen as wilting of the entire plant with the youngest leaves appearing to recover but eventually the whole plant dies.

Leaf_Scorch.quote: Spotted leaves eventually turn brown, dry up, and curl at the margins, giving the leaf an overall burnt or scorched appearance for which the disease is named.
It is common for the petioles of the leaves to have purple, sunken lesions that resemble streaks.

Leaf_Spot.quote: Common leaf spot first appears as small, deep purple spots on the upper surface of leaves.
On petioles, stolons, calyxes, and fruit trusses, elongated lesions may form and interfere with water transport in the plant, weaken the structure, or allow invasion by secondary organisms.

Powdery_Mildew.quote: Early foliar infections are characterized by small white patches of fungus growing on the lower leaf surface, which on susceptible cultivars give these patches a powdery appearance.
The fungus infects flowers which may produce aborted or malformed fruit, and P. aphanis colonizes older fruit, producing fuzzy mycelial growth on the seeds.
